Towards Adaptive, Scalable, and Robust Coordination of LLM Agents:
A Dynamic Ad-Hoc Networking Perspective

Rui Li Affiliation: Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China.    Zeyu Zhang Affiliation: Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China.    Xiaohe Bo Affiliation: Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China.    Quanyu Dai Affiliation: Huawei Technologies Ltd.    Chaozhuo Li Affiliation: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications    Feng Wen Affiliation: Huawei Technologies Ltd.    Xu Chen Affiliation: Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China. Correspondence to:
Abstract

Multi-agent architectures built on large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the potential to realize swarm intelligence through well-crafted collaboration. However, the substantial burden of manual orchestration inherently raises an imperative to automate the design of agentic workflows. We frame such an agent coordination challenge as a classic problem in dynamic ad-hoc networking: How to establish adaptive and reliable communication among a scalable number of agentic hosts? In response to this unresolved dilemma, we introduce RAPS, a reputation-aware publish-subscribe paradigm for adaptive, scalable, and robust coordination of LLM agents. RAPS is grounded in the Distributed Publish-Subscribe Protocol, allowing LLM agents to exchange messages based on their declared intents rather than predefined topologies. Beyond this substrate, RAPS further incorporates two coherent overlays: (i) Reactive Subscription, enabling agents to dynamically refine their intents; and (ii) Bayesian Reputation, empowering each agent with a local watchdog to detect and isolate malicious peers. Extensive experiments over five benchmarks showcase that our design effectively reconciles adaptivity, scalability, and robustness in a unified multi-agent coordination framework.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Multi-agent systems (MAS) (Park et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Tran et al., 2025) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) (Brown et al., 2020; Chowdhery et al., 2023; Dubey et al., 2024) have emerged as a promising avenue towards swarm intelligence, allowing specialized LLM agents (Xi et al., 2025) to collaboratively tackle complex tasks beyond the reach of isolated models (Zhuge et al., 2024). Notably, the efficacy of these systems critically hinges on their underlying coordination architectures (Qian et al., 2024). Early manual orchestration inherently incurs substantial engineering overhead and struggles to generalize across shifting task distributions, thereby underscoring the imperative for automatic multi-agent coordination (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025c; Dang et al., 2025), which empowers the systems to autonomously orchestrate agentic workflows without human intervention.

In this paper, we approach the challenge of automatic coordination through the perspective of computer networking. Given their strong capabilities, LLM agents effectively function as network hosts that can perceive, process, and forward information. Drawing this parallel, the coordination of LLM agents then naturally aligns with dynamic ad-hoc networking (Ramanathan and Redi, 2002; Baldoni and Virgillito, 2005): a set of agentic hosts actively communicate on demand without centralized control, while these hosts may join, leave, or misbehave. Such an analogy directly informs our desiderata: an ideal automatic MAS should (i) adapt to evolving message flow during execution, (ii) scale with dynamic membership discovery, and (iii) remain robust under misbehaving participants. These three requirements—adaptivity, scalability, and robustness—form a tightly coupled design space.

However, existing automatic coordination methods explore only parts of this design space, yet neither resolves the triad simultaneously. Prior works shown in Figure 1(a) typically search for a specific agentic workflow (Zhuge et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c) or train a parameterized coordination network (Zhang et al., 2025b; Shen et al., 2025) based on an offline validation set. This paradigm imposes a fixed connectivity pattern independent of actual communication content (i.e., communication-agnostic), rendering the system blind to the evolving message flow during inference. Moreover, it lacks support for dynamic agent membership, forcing re-orchestration from scratch as agents join or leave. While several recent advances (Ke et al., 2025; Dang et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025), as depicted in Figure 1(b), leverage a high-level meta-controller (e.g., a powerful LLM) to enable inference-time orchestration, their reliance on centralized control inherently incurs the single-point-of-failure bottleneck: If the high-authority meta-controller is compromised, the whole network may malfunction or even collapse, without effective mechanisms for recovery. Therefore, a critical dilemma arises: How to reconcile adaptivity, scalability, and robustness within a unified coordination framework, without heavy training overhead or fragile central control?

In light of this dilemma, we introduce RAPS, a Reputation-Aware Publish-Subscribe paradigm to establish the adaptive, scalable, and robust coordination among LLM-based agents, as shown in Figure 1(c). Instead of enforcing a static topology, RAPS grounds its coordination fabric in a Distributed Publish-Subscribe Protocol (Baldoni and Virgillito, 2005; Frey and Roman, 2007; Yoo et al., 2009), which functionally decouples each agent host into three modules: a Subscriber to state the agent’s intents (i.e., subscriptions); a Publisher to execute the agentic function and generate new messages (i.e., publications); and a Broker to direct information flow by matching publications with content-aligned subscriptions. This intent-based communication protocol serves as an adaptive substrate that liberates the agents from rigid interactions, fostering an open information marketplace where collaboration emerges spontaneously. Building on the basic substrate, our RAPS framework further integrates two overlay mechanisms: (i) Reactive Subscription, empowering the agents to refine their subscriptions for dynamic intent evolution; and (ii) Bayesian Reputation, equipping each agent with a local watchdog to assess peer reliability via Bayesian estimation for trustworthy decentralized collaboration. By combining the publish-subscribe substrate and the overlay mechanisms, RAPS effectively reconciles the critical demands of adaptivity, scalability, and robustness within a unified framework.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Perspective: We frame the MAS coordination problem from a new perspective of dynamic ad-hoc networking, illuminating the key challenge of reconciling adaptivity, scalability, and robustness within a unified framework.

  • •

    Communication Substrate: We propose a Distributed Publish-Subscribe Protocol as the coordination fabric. This protocol functionally decouples LLM agents into intent-declaring Subscribers and message-generating Publishers, liberating the system from rigid topologies to foster spontaneous content-centric collaboration.

  • •

    Overlay Mechanisms: We further design two critical mechanisms to augment the communication substrate: Reactive Subscription and Bayesian Reputation, where the former facilitates dynamic intent evolution and the latter enforces trustworthy decentralized collaboration.

  • •

    Evaluation: Extensive experiments across five diverse benchmarks demonstrate that our holistic RAPS framework effectively reconciles adaptivity, scalability, and robustness for multi-agent coordination, with consistent performance improvements over existing methods.

2 Background

From LLM Agents to MAS. The evolution of LLMs has catalyzed a paradigm shift from passive response generation to autonomous agents capable of perception, reasoning, and action (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). While single-agent models excel at isolated tasks, they typically struggle with complex problems that require diverse expertise or intricate planning (Zhuge et al., 2024). Inspired by the “Society of Mind” theory (Minsky, 1986), early frameworks such as CAMEL (Li et al., 2023), MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2024), and ChatDev (Qian et al., 2023) employ role-playing mechanisms or standard operating procedures to facilitate collaboration. However, these systems primarily rely on hard-coded rules and linear chains, lacking the flexibility to handle dynamic task requirements.

Communication-Agnostic Automatic Coordination. To mitigate the burden of manual engineering, a growing body of research focuses on automating the coordination of LLM agents. Pioneering works such as GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024) model agent interactions as computation graphs, employing evolutionary algorithms to search for optimal connectivity patterns on a validation set. Similarly, some frameworks like ADAS (Hu et al., 2025) and AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025c) utilize search-based optimization to discover effective workflows, while G-Designer (Zhang et al., 2025b) and EIB-Learner (Shen et al., 2025) train a graph neural network to model interaction patterns. These methods decouple the topology orchestration from inference-time communication, inherently inducing rigid agentic workflows regardless of the specific inference context. Such a communication-agnostic strategy not only hinders the adaptivity to evolving message flow, but also impedes the scalability of candidate agents, as agent membership changes would render the pre-wired topologies obsolete, incurring substantial re-optimization costs.

Meta-Controlled Automatic Coordination. To address the rigidity of communication-agnostic coordination, a parallel stream of research adopts a centralized control paradigm to govern the agent communication. Recent advances such as AutoAgents (Chen et al., 2023), MAS-Zero (Ke et al., 2025), and Puppeteer (Dang et al., 2025) leverage a high-authority meta-planner to actively oversee the entire agent interactions and direct the message flow during inference. While such an inference-time orchestration strategy enables message-level adaptivity to some extent, its efficacy is tightly bound to the meta-controller’s capabilities (Dang et al., 2025), incurring a robustness problem of single-point-of-failure. Furthermore, this centralized dependency also imposes a severe bottleneck on scalability, as the decision space for the meta-controller expands combinatorially as the agent population increases.

In contrast to these methods, RAPS shifts the coordination paradigm from offline topology search or fragile centralized control to a distributed intent-centric communication fabric. By grounding LLM agent interactions in a publish-subscribe substrate enriched with two overlay mechanisms, our RAPS fosters spontaneous collaboration based on dynamic intents and peer trust, effectively reconciling adaptivity, scalability, and robustness within a unified framework. Extended discussions on broader related works are provided in Appendix B.

3 LLM Agent Coordination as Dynamic Ad-Hoc Networking

In this section, we formalize the multi-agent coordination problem and establish its correspondence with Dynamic Ad-Hoc Networking. This perspective illuminates three critical desiderata (i.e., Adaptivity, Scalability, and Robustness) that current coordination methods fail to satisfy simultaneously.

3.1 Problem Formulation

We formulate the multi-agent system as a dynamic population of agentic hosts 𝒜={a1,…,aN}\mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{N}\}. Each host ai∈𝒜a_{i}\in\mathcal{A} operates under an LLM-driven policy πθi\pi_{\theta_{i}}. The operational context of πθi\pi_{\theta_{i}} is encapsulated by a configuration tuple 𝒞i=⟨Si,Hi,𝒯i⟩\mathcal{C}_{i}=\\ \langle S_{i},H_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i}\rangle, where SiS_{i} denotes the system prompt specifying the role or function of aia_{i}, HiH_{i} represents the memory buffer storing the accumulated knowledge and interaction history of aia_{i}, and 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} is a collection of external tools available to aia_{i}. Given a complex task query qq, the objective of the system is to synthesize a solution through a collaborative process.

At any discrete time step tt, the agent aia_{i} observes the current state of its local context Hi(t)H_{i}^{(t)} and then generates a message mi(t)∼πθi(⋅|Si,Hi(t),𝒯i)m_{i}^{(t)}\sim\pi_{\theta_{i}}(\cdot|S_{i},H_{i}^{(t)},\mathcal{T}_{i}). The core challenge of MAS design centers on the coordination function Φ\Phi, which governs the dissemination scope of this new message:

ℛi(t+1)=Φ⁡(mi(t),𝒜),where ​ℛi(t+1)⊆𝒜∖{ai}.\mathcal{R}_{i}^{(t+1)}=\Phi(m_{i}^{(t)},\mathcal{A}),\;\text{where }\mathcal{R}_{i}^{(t+1)}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\setminus\{a_{i}\}. (1)

When the new message arrives, each recipient aj∈ℛi(t+1)a_{j}\in\mathcal{R}_{i}^{(t+1)} updates its local context Hj(t+1)←Hj(t)∪{mi(t)}H_{j}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow H_{j}^{(t)}\cup\{m_{i}^{(t)}\} and may subsequently trigger new actions. In contrast to recent works that typically model Φ\Phi as either a static topological mapping (i.e., routing messages on communication-agnostic graphs) or a global orchestration policy (i.e., leveraging a centralized meta-controller to dispatch messages), we rethink the automatic coordination problem from the perspective of dynamic ad-hoc networking, where communication patterns emerge spontaneously based on the semantic intents of each agent.

3.2 Networking Perspective

We posit that the coordination of LLM agents is structurally isomorphic to the operation of dynamic ad-hoc networks (Ramanathan and Redi, 2002). Specifically, we map the basic components of LLM-MAS to classic networking primitives:

  • •

    Hosts (aia_{i}): Each LLM agent functions as an autonomous network host. Under this analogy, the system prompt 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} of aia_{i} defines the host’s service profile; the memory state ℋi(t)\mathcal{H}_{i}^{(t)} acts as the local cache for storing interaction history; and the toolset 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} represents the executable plugins for service.

  • •

    Packets (mi(t)m_{i}^{(t)}): The natural language messages generated by agents serve as information packets carrying semantic payloads. Unlike traditional TCP/IP networks that route packets based on explicit destination addresses (Kessler, 2004), the dissemination of mi(t)m_{i}^{(t)} in dynamic ad-hoc networks is governed by the semantic alignment between its payload and the receivers’ intents (Ahlgren et al., 2012).

  • •

    Topology (𝒢(t)\mathcal{G}^{(t)}): The interaction graph 𝒢(t)\mathcal{G}^{(t)} induced by Φ\Phi naturally reveals a transient communication pattern. In the ad-hoc settings, this topology is decoupled from physical infrastructure, operating instead as a logical overlay that evolves on-the-fly. Links between hosts emerge spontaneously, driven by the shifts in host intents (Yoo et al., 2009) and peer trustworthiness (Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2004).

This mapping also reveals that prevailing MAS orchestration works such as AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025c) and G-Designer (Zhang et al., 2025b) are akin to the legacy circuit-switching networks (Tanenbaum, 2003), which are incompatible with the dynamic information flow of swarm intelligence. To deal with this rigidity, the system necessitates a paradigm shift towards content-centric packet-switching (Eugster et al., 2003), where the routing decisions are decentralized and driven by semantic content rather than pre-established paths.

Design Desiderata. Drawing on the isomorphism between MAS and dynamic ad-hoc networking, we posit an effective coordination design to be one that reconciles three critical properties: (i) Adaptivity requires intent-based communication, where message dissemination is governed by semantic alignment rather than fixed topologies that are agnostic to the evolving message flows (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025c); (ii) Scalability demands the support for dynamic membership (Eugster et al., 2003) to accommodate variable agent populations, avoiding the prohibitive re-optimization overhead of pre-wiring models (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025c) and the combinatorial bottlenecks of centralized meta-controllers (Ke et al., 2025; Dang et al., 2025); (iii) Robustness necessitates a decentralized trust mechanism to insulate the system from adversarial behaviors (Shayegani et al., 2023) and alleviate the single-point-of-failure risks (Ke et al., 2025). Refer to Appendix B for more discussions.

4 RAPS: Reputation-Aware Publish-Subscribe Communication

In this paper, we introduce RAPS, a new MAS coordination framework that simultaneously reconciles the desiderata of adaptivity, scalability, and robustness outlined in Section 3. We first provide an overview of our RAPS framework (§4.1). Subsequently, we elaborate on its communication substrate (§4.2) and two critical overlay mechanisms (§4.3 and §4.4).

4.1 Overview

As illustrated in Figure 2, RAPS fundamentally shifts the coordination paradigm from rigid topology orchestration or fragile centralized control to intent-centric communication.

At its core, RAPS employs a distributed publish-subscribe protocol as the communication substrate, which functionally decouples the agentic hosts into packet producers and consumers, directing the information flow based on the semantic alignment between declared intents (i.e., subscriptions) and produced contents (i.e., publications). By eschewing the pre-wired interaction graphs and the vulnerable central planners, this substrate fosters an open information marketplace for adaptive MAS coordination, while also allowing the agents to seamlessly join or leave without topology reconfiguration.

Building on such a communication substrate, RAPS further incorporates two overlay mechanisms to facilitate dynamic intent evolution and trustworthy decentralized collaboration. Reactive Subscription empowers the agents to dynamically update their intents based on the evolving message contexts, akin to the online prompt optimization (Li et al., 2025b) that can spontaneously adapt to the unfolding interaction history. Bayesian Reputation equips each agent with a local watchdog that maintains probabilistic beliefs about peer reliability to insulates the system from adversarial behaviors, ensuring robust collaboration without recourse to a central authority. By integrating these overlays atop the distributed substrate, RAPS coherently fulfills the desiderata of adaptivity, scalability, and robustness in a unified coordination framework.

4.2 Substrate: Publish-Subscribe Protocol

To dismantle the rigidity of pre-wired interaction topologies, RAPS moves beyond current MAS designs by establishing a distributed publish-subscribe protocol as its communication substrate. This protocol functionally decouples the agentic hosts into message producers (Publishers) and consumers (Subscribers), mediated by a content-aware Broker module.

Three Functional Roles. Formally, we define the operational tuple for each agent ai∈𝒜a_{i}\in\mathcal{A} as ⟨fi𝚂,fi𝙿,fi𝙱⟩\langle f_{i}^{\mathtt{S}},f_{i}^{\mathtt{P}},f_{i}^{\mathtt{B}}\rangle, corresponding to three distinct logical roles:

  • •

    Subscriber (fi𝚂f_{i}^{\mathtt{S}}): This function allows the network host to explicitly declare its packet intents or service capability. In the agentic context, such a subscription naturally aligns with the system prompt SiS_{i} configured when each agent aia_{i} joins the network. For instance, a host initialized with the role “Python Expert” directly broadcasts a standing subscription to the network, signaling its ability to process the publications about code generation or debugging tasks.

  • •

    Publisher (fi𝙿f_{i}^{\mathtt{P}}): The publisher acts as the functional core of agent aia_{i}. At step tt, upon receiving a packet m(t−1)m^{(t-1)} that aligns with its subscription SiS_{i}, the publisher directly runs the base policy πθi\pi_{\theta_{i}} conditioned on its local context buffer ⟨Si,Hi(t−1)∪m(t−1),𝒯i⟩\langle S_{i},H_{i}^{(t-1)}\cup m^{(t-1)},\mathcal{T}_{i}\rangle to produce a new message m(t)m^{(t)}. Note that the publisher does not specify recipients of m(t)m^{(t)}, but rather broadcasts it as a semantic signal for alignment.

  • •

    Broker (fi𝙱f_{i}^{\mathtt{B}}): This module operates as the instantiation of the coordination function Φ\Phi in Equation (1). Unlike prior methods that model Φ\Phi as static lookup or central planning, the broker implements Φ\Phi through decentralized semantic matching: it derives the recipient set ℛi(t+1)\mathcal{R}_{i}^{(t+1)} by assessing the compatibility between the published message mtm_{t} and the global subscription pool 𝒮={Sj}j≠i\mathcal{S}=\{S_{j}\}_{j\neq i}. Such an intent-content bridging process fosters the interaction graph 𝒢(t)\mathcal{G}^{(t)} to emerge spontaneously in response to the task progress.

Coordination Dynamics. With these three functional roles, the basic coordination protocol of RAPS alternates between Publication and Brokerage to induce the interaction patterns.

Publication Phase. At any time step tt, RAPS operates on a set of active agents ℛ∗(t)\mathcal{R}_{*}^{(t)}. For the initial step (t=0t=0), ℛinit(0)\mathcal{R}_{\text{init}}^{(0)} is populated with default entry roles (e.g., an Analyst agent) activated directly by the input query qq, whereas ℛ∗(t)\mathcal{R}_{*}^{(t)} for the subsequent steps is inherited from the preceding brokerage outcomes. Every active agent ai∈ℛ∗(t)a_{i}\in\mathcal{R}_{*}^{(t)} first aggregates the received message packets ℳi(t−1)={m∗(t−1)∣ai∈ℛ∗(t)}\mathcal{M}_{i}^{(t-1)}=\{m_{*}^{(t-1)}\mid a_{i}\in\mathcal{R}_{*}^{(t)}\} to update its interaction context. Then, aia_{i} runs the publisher function fi𝙿f_{i}^{\mathtt{P}} to produce the new publication:

mi(t)=fi𝙿​(Si,Hi(t−1)∪ℳi(t−1)).m_{i}^{(t)}=f_{i}^{\mathtt{P}}\!\left(S_{i},~H_{i}^{(t-1)}\cup\mathcal{M}_{i}^{(t-1)}\right). (2)

In practice, fi𝙿f_{i}^{\mathtt{P}} is typically instantiated as the LLM backbone πθi\pi_{\theta_{i}} of aia_{i}. The publication mi(t)m_{i}^{(t)} serves as a flexible semantic container modulated by the output instructions of policy πθi\pi_{\theta_{i}}, capable of explicitly encapsulating the chain-of-thought reasoning (Wei et al., 2022), intermediate execution results, and strategic plans intended for subsequent interactions.

Brokerage Phase. Upon the publication of mi(t)m_{i}^{(t)}, the control flow shifts to the broker fi𝙱f_{i}^{\mathtt{B}} to determine dissemination path for this message. The broker treats mi(t)m_{i}^{(t)} as a query to search for compatible consumers within the standing subscriptions 𝒮\mathcal{S} of other hosts. Formally, for each producer aia_{i}, its broker identifies a subset of recipients ℛi(t+1)\mathcal{R}_{i}^{(t+1)}:

ℛi(t+1)=fi𝙱​(mi(t),𝒮)⊆𝒜.\mathcal{R}_{i}^{(t+1)}=f_{i}^{\mathtt{B}}\!\left(m_{i}^{(t)},\mathcal{S}\right)\subseteq\mathcal{A}. (3)

In practice, the instantiation of fi𝙱f_{i}^{\mathtt{B}} spans a spectrum of complexity, ranging from lightweight embedding-based scoring to expressive LLM-driven selection. Such brokers can only determine one recipient each time to produce dynamic chain topology (Dang et al., 2025) for simple scenarios, while also retaining the flexibility to activate multiple subscribers simultaneously for complex problem solving (Li et al., 2025a).

Termination. This publication-brokerage process terminates when the active agents emit a consensus finish signal or the maximum time step limit is reached. Finally, the system aggregates all publications and delegating one terminal agent to provide the final answer (Jiang et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b).

This intent-driven substrate naturally establishes an adaptive and scalable communication fabric by liberating message flow from static topology. Notably, the raw protocol neither accounts for the evolving granularity of agent subscriptions nor guards against potential misbehavior in an open system. To bridge these gaps, we further augment this substrate with two coherent overlay mechanisms: reactive subscription for dynamic intent evolution (§4.3) and Bayesian reputation for trustworthy decentralized collaboration (§4.4).

4.3 Overlay I: Reactive Subscription

Under the substrate protocol, LLM agents act as static hosts with fixed subscriptions (i.e., system prompts) initialized at their joining time. However, such seed subscriptions may be too abstract or even absent for the emerging message types.

To improve the intent-content alignment without introducing centralized control, RAPS augments the basic substrate with a lightweight mechanism of Reactive Subscription, allowing each active agent to refine its standing subscription based on the newly received packets before the publication phase.

Reactive Subscription. At time step tt, each active host ai∈ℛ∗(t)a_{i}\in\mathcal{R}_{*}^{(t)} first updates its system profile Si(t−1)S_{i}^{(t-1)} according to the latest messages ℳi(t−1)\mathcal{M}_{i}^{(t-1)} and optionally its context Hi(t−1)H_{i}^{(t-1)}:

Si(t)=fi𝚂​(Si(t−1),Hi(t−1)∪ℳi(t−1)),S_{i}^{(t)}=f^{\mathtt{S}}_{i}\!\left(S_{i}^{(t-1)},\,H_{i}^{(t-1)}\cup\mathcal{M}_{i}^{(t-1)}\right), (4)

where fi𝚂f_{i}^{\mathtt{S}} is instantiated as an LLM-driven prompt rewriter that specializes the seed subscription by identifying salient intents, constraints, or tool cues from the received messages. Such an updated Si(t)S_{i}^{(t)} then directly conditions the subsequent publication in Equation (2), replacing the static prompt with the reactive one, so that the next message is generated under a more context-aware role to improve the functional quality. Moreover, RAPS can optionally promote the transient local profile Si(t)S_{i}^{(t)} into the global subscription pool 𝒮\mathcal{S} under certain confirmation signals (e.g., peer acknowledgments in the next subsection), thus coherently realizing dynamic membership discovery without any centralized topology reconfiguration.

4.4 Overlay II: Bayesian Reputation

While the reactive subscription mechanism improves intent-content alignment, the open-ended communication substrate of RAPS remains vulnerable to unreliable behaviors such as hallucinations (Huang et al., 2025), tool misuse (Fu et al., 2024), or adversarial manipulation (Shayegani et al., 2023). To secure the coordination without reverting to a centralized global judge, RAPS presents a fully decentralized Bayesian Reputation Overlay inspired by classic robustness designs (Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2002; Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2004) in ad-hoc networks.

Distributed Watchdog. RAPS equips each agent aia_{i} with a local watchdog that maintains pairwise probabilistic beliefs about every peer aja_{j} it interacts with. Concretely, the watchdog of aia_{i} holds three probabilistic ratings for aja_{j}, including First-Hand Rating Fi​jF_{ij} that indicates aia_{i}’s direct evaluation of aja_{j}’s behavioral quality; Trust Rating Ti​jT_{ij} that quantifies how much aia_{i} trusts aja_{j} as a reporter of reputation evidences; and the overall reputation Pi​jP_{ij} that aggregates direct evaluation and indirect reports into the final belief about aja_{j}’s reliability.

Bayesian Modeling. Since LLM agents operate with sparse, noisy, and non-stationary context, the point estimates of peer reliability can be brittle. To draw uncertainty-aware beliefs, we cast each rating as a Bayesian posterior over an underlying Bernoulli parameter associated with the evidence stream. Following the classic settings (Davison, 2003; Berger, 2013), we then use the conjugate Beta-Bernoulli model to represent the uncertainty of each rating with two pseudo-counts:

Fi​j=β⁡(xi​jF,yi​jF),Ti​j=β⁡(xi​jT,yi​jT),Pi​j=β⁡(xi​jP,yi​jP).\displaystyle F_{ij}=\beta(x^{F}_{ij},y^{F}_{ij}),\ T_{ij}=\beta(x^{T}_{ij},y^{T}_{ij}),\ P_{ij}=\beta(x^{P}_{ij},y^{P}_{ij}).

 (5)

Here Fi​jF_{ij} and Pi​jP_{ij} summarize aja_{j}’s behavioral reliability as a publication source, while Ti​jT_{ij} represents the credibility of aja_{j}, each driven by its corresponding Bernoulli evidence stream.

All ratings start from a non-informative prior β⁡(1,1)\beta(1,1), and are updated incrementally as the new observation si​j∗s_{ij}^{*} arrives. Since agent behaviors and task regimes may drift over time, we adopt a discounted update that emphasizes the recent si​j∗s_{ij}^{*}:​

xi​j∗←λ​xi​j∗+si​j∗,yi​j∗←λ​yi​j∗+(1−si​j∗),x_{ij}^{*}\leftarrow\lambda\,x_{ij}^{*}+s_{ij}^{*},\qquad y_{ij}^{*}\leftarrow\lambda\,y_{ij}^{*}+(1-s_{ij}^{*}), (6)

where si​j∗s_{ij}^{*} denotes the corresponding binary evidence for the specific rating to be updated (i.e., ∗∈{F,T,R}*\in\{F,T,R\}); λ∈(0,1]\lambda\in(0,1] represents a decay factor applied to the past pseudo-counts. The posterior mean 𝔼⁡[β⁡(xi​j∗,yi​j∗)]=xi​j∗/(xi​j∗+yi​j∗)\mathbb{E}[\beta(x^{*}_{ij},y^{*}_{ij})]=x^{*}_{ij}/(x^{*}_{ij}+y^{*}_{ij}) offers a calibrated point estimate, while the concentration (xi​j∗+yi​j∗)(x^{*}_{ij}+y^{*}_{ij}) also reflects epistemic uncertainty for downstream decisions.​

Reputation Calculation. Based on the Bayesian modeling, RAPS calculates each rating by instantiating the Bernoulli evidence stream during coordination. When aia_{i} routes a message to a downstream agent aja_{j}, the local watchdog of aia_{i} (i) performs a first-hand evaluation on the publication of aja_{j}, (ii) selectively collects second-hand testimonials from other witnesses and assesses their credibility to update trust, and (iii) merges admissible direct/indirect evidence into the final reputation posterior that fuels the reputation-aware brokers.

First-Hand Evaluation. Whenever aia_{i} receives a publication from aja_{j}, the local watchdog of aia_{i} (e.g., an LLM auditor) performs an on-the-fly verification to produce a first-hand binary evaluation score si​jF∈{0,1}s^{F}_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. Concretely, si​jF=0s^{F}_{ij}=0 if the publication of aja_{j} is judged useful and consistent with its current context; otherwise si​jF=1s^{F}_{ij}=1 if the watchdog detects qualified misbehaviors such as factual error and tool misuse:

si​jF=fi𝙳​(mj(t),Si(t),Hi(t))∈{0,1},s^{F}_{ij}=f_{i}^{\mathtt{D}}\!\left(m_{j}^{(t)},\,S_{i}^{(t)},\,H_{i}^{(t)}\right)\in\{0,1\}, (7)

where fi𝙳f_{i}^{\mathtt{D}} denotes the watchdog function of aia_{i}. The evidence si​jFs^{F}_{ij} is then used to update the first-hand posterior Fi​j=β⁡(xi​jF,yi​jF)F_{ij}=\beta(x^{F}_{ij},y^{F}_{ij}) via the discounted rule in Equation (6), yielding a direct rationality summary of aja_{j} from the perspective of aia_{i}.​

Second-Hand Witness. While first-hand evaluation anchors reputation to verifiable local evidence, relying solely on si​jFs^{F}_{ij} can be sample-inefficient in open coordination (Michiardi and Molva, 2002). To accelerate the discovery of unreliable peers, RAPS allows aia_{i} to optionally solicit second-hand testimonies from other witnesses that have recently interacted with aja_{j}. Concretely, upon receiving mj(t)m_{j}^{(t)}, aia_{i} queries a small set of witnesses 𝒲i​j(t)⊆𝒜∖{ai,aj}\mathcal{W}_{ij}^{(t)}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\setminus\{a_{i},a_{j}\} and obtains their first-hand posteriors about aja_{j}, i.e., {Fk​j=β(xk​jF,yk​jF)}ak∈𝒲i​j(t)\{F_{kj}=\beta(x^{F}_{kj},y^{F}_{kj})\}_{a_{k}\in\mathcal{W}_{ij}^{(t)}}. Since second-hand reports may be noisy or malicious, aia_{i} evaluates each witness aka_{k} by performing a deviation test (Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2004) on its current belief Pi​jP_{ij}:

|𝔼⁡[Fk​j]−𝔼⁡[Pi​j]|Var​(Fk​j)+Var​(Pi​j)≥δ,\frac{\left|\mathbb{E}[F_{kj}]-\mathbb{E}[P_{ij}]\right|}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(F_{kj})+\text{Var}(P_{ij})}}\geq\delta, (8)

where δ\delta is a predefined tolerance threshold. If the deviation exceeds δ\delta, the testimony is deemed incompatible (yielding evidence si​kT=1s^{T}_{ik}=1); otherwise, it is accepted (si​kT=0s^{T}_{ik}=0). This binary evidence is then used to update the trust posterior Ti​kT_{ik} via Eq. (6), progressively isolating dishonest witnesses.

Reputation Merging. To synthesize a holistic view of peer reliability, aia_{i} aggregates its direct evidence si​jFs^{F}_{ij} with indirect testimonies into the cumulative reputation posterior Pi​jP_{ij} via linear pool model merging (Berger, 2013). First, Pi​jP_{ij} is anchored to the first-hand evidence si​jFs^{F}_{ij}, directly updating the parameters (xi​jP,yi​jP)(x^{P}_{ij},y^{P}_{ij}) with Eq. (6). Then, aia_{i} incorporates second-hand reports from a subset of admissible witnesses 𝒲i​j∗⊆𝒲i​j(t)\mathcal{W}^{*}_{ij}\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{ij}^{(t)}. Following the classic protocol (Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2004), a witness aka_{k} is deemed admissible if it is either locally trusted (i.e., 𝔼⁡[Ti​k]≥τ\mathbb{E}[T_{ik}]\geq\tau) or its testimony successfully passes the deviation test (i.e., si​kT=0s^{T}_{ik}=0). For every ak∈𝒲i​j∗a_{k}\in\mathcal{W}^{*}_{ij}, we assimilate its reported posterior Fk​j=β⁡(xk​jF,yk​jF)F_{kj}=\beta(x^{F}_{kj},y^{F}_{kj}) as weak pseudo-counts to refine the local belief:

xi​jP←xi​jP+ω​xk​jF,yi​jP←yi​jP+ω​yk​jF,x^{P}_{ij}\leftarrow x^{P}_{ij}+\omega\,x^{F}_{kj},\qquad y^{P}_{ij}\leftarrow y^{P}_{ij}+\omega\,y^{F}_{kj}, (9)

where ω∈(0,1)\omega\in(0,1) is a discounting factor. Such a merging mechanism ensures that indirect evidence can modulate but does not overwhelm first-hand observations, resulting in a trust-gated aggregation that is robust to reputation poisoning.​

Reputation-Aware Brokerage. With the reputation overlay, the broker of aia_{i} evolves to be reliability-aware, thus enabling us to rewrite the brokerage function in Equation (3) as:

ℛi(t+1)=fi𝙱​(mi(t),𝒮,𝒫i)⊆𝒜,\mathcal{R}_{i}^{(t+1)}=f_{i}^{\mathtt{B}}\!\left(m_{i}^{(t)},\,\mathcal{S},\,\mathcal{P}_{i}\right)\subseteq\mathcal{A}, (10)

where 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} denotes aia_{i}’s local reputation table. As a result, the information flow is steered away from untrusted hosts, preventing local failures from cascading into global corruption.

5 Experiments

To comprehensively validate the effectiveness of our RAPS framework, we conduct extensive experiments on a range of representative agent tasks spanning general reasoning, mathematical problem solving, and code generation. In the main experiment (§5.2), we compare RAPS with strong baselines over five heterogeneous benchmarks to assess its adaptivity. Then, we vary the number of agents to study scalability and efficiency under open-ended memberships (§5.3). Next, we stress-test robustness (§5.4) by injecting adversarial agents. Finally, the detailed mechanism analysis is provided in §5.5.

5.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks. We evaluate RAPS over five standard datasets from three categories: MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020) for general reasoning; GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), SVAMP (Patel et al., 2021), and AQuA (Ling et al., 2017) for mathematical reasoning; HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) for code generation. We report Pass@1 for HumanEval and accuracy (Acc.) for others. See Appendix D for the detailed statistics.

Baselines. We compare RAPS with four types of baselines, including (1) Single-Agent Models: CoT (Wei et al., 2022), ComplexCoT (Fu et al., 2022), and Self-Consistency (abbr. SC) (Wang et al., 2022); (2) Static Multi-Agent Models: MacNet (Chain, Star, Tree, Random) (Qian et al., 2024), LLM-Debate (Du et al., 2023), and LLM-Blender (Jiang et al., 2023); (3) Communication-Agnostic Coordination: GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024), AgentPrune (Zhang et al., 2024), AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025c), MaAS (Zhang et al., 2025a), and G-Designer (Zhang et al., 2025b); (4) Meta-Controlled Coordination: AutoAgents (Chen et al., 2023), Puppeteer (Dang et al., 2025), MAS-Zero (Ke et al., 2025).

Implementation Details. Unless otherwise specified, we use GPT-4o-mini as the LLM backbone model across all methods to ensure fair comparisons. For the agentic profiles in MAS, we adopt the standard role definitions and system prompt configurations following previous works (Liu et al., 2024; Zhuge et al., 2024). For our RAPS framework, we instantiate the publishers fi𝙿f_{i}^{\mathtt{P}}, reactive subscribers fi𝚂f_{i}^{\mathtt{S}}, and local watchdogs fi𝙳f_{i}^{\mathtt{D}} using the same LLM backbone. The broker fi𝙱f_{i}^{\mathtt{B}} is implemented to support both embedding-based matching with text-embedding-3-small for efficiency and LLM-based reasoning for complex decisions. More implementation details are provided in Appendix E.

5.2 Main Results

The performance comparison on five benchmarks is reported in Table 1. RAPS achieves state-of-the-art performance across all tasks, attaining the highest average score of 90.0%. We attribute these advanced gains to the message-level adaptivity of RAPS compared to existing paradigms:

Superiority over Static Structures. The static models (e.g., Chain, Star) often lag behind even single-agent baselines (e.g., Chain is 4.9% lower than CoT on SVAMP), indicating that rigid topologies cannot accommodate the diverse reasoning patterns required by different queries. RAPS overcomes this limitation by allowing the interaction graph to emerge dynamically. The intent-based publish-subscribe substrate ensures that messages are routed to relevant agents, avoiding the structural mismatch inherent in static graphs.

Advantages over Offline Optimization. Communication-agnostic methods such as AFlow and G-Designer search for or generate workflows without considering specific communication process. Despite their effectiveness, such methods remain blind to the evolving message flow during inference. Beyond these baselines, RAPS framework achieves superior performance (e.g., +3.2% over G-Designer on AQuA) with its inherent capacity for inference-time coordination. Moreover, the agents in RAPS can further tailor their roles to the message context via reactive subscription, thereby capturing subtle reasoning paths overlooked by the pre-wired models.

Comparison with Centralized Control. Meta-controlled architectures (e.g., AutoAgents, Puppeteer, and MAS-Zero) rely on a central planner, inherently inducing a performance bottleneck due to the complexity of global state supervision. RAPS surpasses these models (e.g., +5.0% over AutoAgents on average) by distributing the routing logic. Departing from a monolithic agent that dictates holistic connectivity, RAPS decentralizes the routing logic by empowering local brokers to adaptively align publications with relevant subscriptions, leading to more nuanced and effective collaboration patterns.​

5.3 Scalability and Efficiency

A critical requirement for dynamic ad-hoc networking is the ability to scale effectively as the number of hosts increases. We evaluate the scalability and efficiency of RAPS by varying the agent population size NN on the MMLU benchmark.

Population Scalability. Figure 3(a) shows the performance (accuracy) of each method as the agent population increases. The chain model suffers from severe accuracy degradation due to error propagation across increasing interaction hops. Similarly, the Puppeteer model also fails to maintain performance, since its central orchestrator struggles to analyze and coordinate among the growing number of agents. In contrast, RAPS consistently outperforms such approaches, exhibiting steady accuracy gains with the increasing number of agents. This demonstrates the scalability of our distributed publish-subscribe protocol, confirming its ability to handle growing agent populations without compromising performance.

Communication Efficiency. Figure 3(b) further reports the end-to-end runtime as the agent population scales. The two communication-agnostic approaches (i.e., GPTSwarm and G-Designer) inherently incur rapidly growing optimization overhead (over 2 hours for 20 agents) as the agent candidate pool expands. In comparison, RAPS is training-free and performs coordination entirely at inference time via lightweight publish-subscribe matching. Moreover, the broker-selective dissemination effectively prevents unnecessary interactions, thereby keeping the inference latency stable as NN increases. As a result, RAPS achieves favorable runtime scaling while simultaneously improving accuracy, demonstrating an efficient coordination substrate for open-membership systems.

Cost-Performance Trade-off. Furthermore, we analyze the economic viability of our RAPS in Figure 4, which plots the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus token consumption on three representative benchmarks. The green curve presents the performance of RAPS at varying communication rounds k∈{3,5,7,10}k\in\{3,5,7,10\}. One can observe that RAPS establishes a superior frontier compared to the state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its advantages in both accuracy and efficiency.

5.4 Robustness Analysis

In open multi-agent systems, agents may exhibit unreliable behaviors due to hallucinations or adversarial attacks. To evaluate robustness, we conduct a “Byzantine” stress test on the MMLU benchmark by injecting adversarial agents prompted to provide misleading reasoning. We vary the composition of the agent pool from clean (5 Truthful, 0 Adversarial) to highly contaminated (2 Truthful, 3 Adversarial, or a mix of 5T5A). The results are summarized in Table 2.

Fragility of Baselines. Existing models exhibit severe vulnerability to adversarial interference. For instance, AFlow and GPTSwarm experience sharp drops in accuracy when adversarial agents are introduced, with accuracy plummeting to as low as 19.6% under the 2T3A scenario. Moreover, Puppeteer, which relies on a centralized meta-controller, is susceptible to adversarial attacks in two different configurations: one where the adversarial prompt targets the non-central agents, and another where the adversarial prompt is aimed at the central meta-controller itself. In the latter case, we observe that Puppeteer-C collapses immediately (84.3% →\to 13.7%) with just one adversarial agent (4T1A), confirming that entrusting a monolithic high-authority controller is inherently unsafe for open coordination.

Efficacy of Bayesian Reputation. In contrast, RAPS consistently outperforms all other methods, maintaining high accuracy even as the number of adversarial agents increases. The performance of RAPS with and without Bayesian Reputation (BR) shows that the inclusion of BR can significantly enhance communication robustness, ensuring stable performance even in the contaminated agent pools. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of BR in maintaining system reliability under adversarial conditions.

5.5 Ablation Analysis

To understand the contribution of each component within RAPS, we conduct an ablation study on MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval, as presented in Table 3 and Figure 5.

Impact of Overlay Mechanisms. We evaluate the impact of removing the two designed overlay mechanisms: Reactive Subscription (RS) and Bayesian Reputation (BR). As shown in Table 3, removing RS leads to a notable performance drop, highlighting the importance of dynamic subscriptions in adapting to the task dynamics; similarly, removing BR also incurs a moderate decline, as the reputation-aware brokerage can enhance the communication quality by filtering out low-quality reasoning signals. Therefore, these two mechanisms contribute synergistically to the full performance of RAPS.

Broker Instantiation. We compare the default embedding-based broker with a more expressive LLM-based broker (w/ LLM Broker). While the LLM broker yields marginal performance improvements (e.g., +1.3% on MMLU), it would inherently incur higher communication latency. This justifies our design choice of using the embedding-based broker for the main experiments to balance efficiency and accuracy.

Resilience to Agent Pool Quality. A common limitation of current models is their sensitivity to the quality of initial agent configurations. We investigate this by comparing the model performance on a Crafted Pool (expert roles) versus a Naive Pool (generic roles). As shown in Figure 5, existing models suffer severe degradation when using the naive pool. For instance, G-Designer drops by 9.5% (91.0% →\to 81.5%). In contrast, RAPS exhibits remarkable resilience, maintaining robust performance with only a negligible 1.3% drop (91.5% →\to 90.2%). This resilience is directly attributable to the Reactive Subscription mechanism, which allows even naively initialized agents to autonomously refine their intents and specialize their roles based on the message context.

6 Conclusion

This paper re-envisions the coordination of LLM agents through the lens of dynamic ad-hoc networking, identifying the critical challenge of simultaneously achieving adaptivity, scalability, and robustness. To address this dilemma, we introduced RAPS, a decentralized framework grounded in a reputation-aware publish-subscribe protocol. By decoupling coordination from rigid topologies and fragile centralized controllers, RAPS empowers agents to spontaneously align their intents with evolving tasks and autonomously isolate unreliable peers via a distributed trust mechanism. Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that RAPS effectively reconciles the coordination triad, yielding state-of-the-art performance while scaling efficiently to larger agent populations and exhibiting superior resilience against adversarial interference. We believe this networking-centric perspective provides a robust foundation for building open, self-organizing, and trustworthy multi-agent societies.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

Appendix B Discussion on Related Works

In the main text, we established an isomorphism between Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) and dynamic ad-hoc networks. In this appendix, we provide a detailed taxonomic review of existing literature through the specific lens of network topology and communication protocols (Tanenbaum, 2003). This perspective highlights the structural limitations of prior works and positions RAPS as a necessary evolution towards dynamic ad-hoc networking for LLM agents.

Static Topologies: Hardwired Circuits

The earliest and most prevalent form of multi-agent coordination mirrors the legacy circuit-switching paradigm in telecommunications, where communication channels are pre-established and remain fixed for the duration of a session. Approaches such as CoT (Wei et al., 2022), though originally designed for single models, laid the groundwork for sequential multi-agent workflows like Camel (Li et al., 2023) and ChatDev (Qian et al., 2023). In these systems, information flows through a hard-coded sequence of roles (e.g., User →\to Programmer →\to Tester). While easy to implement, these linear topologies suffer from the single-path dependency: a failure or hallucination at any node propagates downstream without recourse for error correction, analogous to a cut wire in a circuit-switched network.

Graph Search/Optimization: Circuit Switching

To address the limitations of static topologies, recent models such as GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024), AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025c), and G-Designer (Zhang et al., 2025b) employ optimization algorithms (e.g., genetic algorithms or gradient-based evolution) to discover interaction graphs. While these methods generate more complex topologies (e.g., DAGs or Trees), they remain communication-agnostic during inference. Consequently, these systems cannot reroute messages dynamically when an agent encounters an unexpected sub-problem, nor can they handle scalability regarding dynamic membership, as adding a new agent requires re-running the expensive optimization process.

Centralized Orchestration: Software-Defined Networking

A parallel line of research adopts a centralized paradigm, conceptually similar to Software-Defined Networking (Kreutz et al., 2014), where a central controller dictates the forwarding plane. These meta-controlled frameworks like AutoAgents (Chen et al., 2023), Puppeteer (Dang et al., 2025), and MAS-Zero (Ke et al., 2025) utilize a high-capacity LLM to decompose tasks and route messages to specific agents. While this paradigm introduces a degree of runtime adaptivity, it incurs the severe robustness vulnerability of Single Point of Failure (SPoF). If the central planner hallucinates or is compromised via prompt injection, the entire coordination fabric collapses. Furthermore, this centralization also imposes a computational bottleneck that hinders scalability, as the context window and reasoning complexity of the controller grow combinatorially with the number of agents.

Consensus-Based Debate: Broadcast Flooding

Moving towards decentralization, several frameworks utilize peer-to-peer interactions without a central authority, while focusing on consensus building. These LLM Debate (Du et al., 2023; Estornell and Liu, 2024) methods allow agents to critique each other’s outputs to converge on a solution. From a networking perspective, these approaches often rely on broadcasting (all-to-all communication) or rigid round-robin scheduling. While robust against individual errors, such broadcasting incurs high communication overhead (message complexity of 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2})) and noise accumulation. In contrast, RAPS employs the Publish-Subscribe Protocol that functions as semantic multicasting to deliver messages only to interested subscribers, thereby reconciling decentralized inference with communication efficiency.

Our RAPS Framework: Dynamic Ad-Hoc Networking

Departing from the aforementioned paradigms, RAPS frames the multi-agent coordination challenge through the perspective of Dynamic Ad-Hoc Networking, specifically aligning with the principles in Content-Centric Networks (CCN) (Baldoni and Virgillito, 2005; Frey and Roman, 2007; Yoo et al., 2009) and Mobile Ad-Hoc Networks (MANETs) (Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2002; Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2004).

  • •

    Content-Centric vs. Host-Centric: Traditional MAS approaches (both static and centralized) operate on a host-centric model, where messages are addressed to specific agent identities (e.g., “Send to Analyst”). RAPS adopts a content-centric approach via the Publish-Subscribe protocol (Frey and Roman, 2007). Routing decisions are driven by the semantic match between the message payload (publication) and agent intents (subscriptions), decoupling the information producer from the consumer. This mirrors the shift in modern networking from IP-based routing to Named Data Networking (NDN) (Ahlgren et al., 2012), allowing the system to focus on what is being exchanged rather than who is exchanging it.

  • •

    Reactive Subscription: While graph search/optimization methods (e.g., GPTSwarm) rely on offline topology generation, RAPS implements reactive routing akin to the on-demand protocols in ad-hoc networks (e.g., AODV (Ramanathan and Redi, 2002)). Through the Reactive Subscription mechanism, agents update their “interest profiles” in real-time based on the evolving context, effectively repairing and optimizing communication paths on the fly without global reconfiguration.

  • •

    Bayesian Reputation: Moreover, RAPS integrates the Bayesian Reputation mechanism to address the security vulnerabilities of open systems. This draws a direct parallel to distributed watchdog and reputation systems in MANETs (Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2002; Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2004), where nodes cooperatively detect and isolate misbehaving peers based on local observation and second-hand testimonials, thereby achieving robustness without a centralized firewall.

Summary

We summarize the networking analogies of different MAS coordination paradigms in Table 5. While previous works have explored specific points in the design space—ranging from rigid circuit-switched chains to vulnerable centralized controllers—RAPS represents the first cohesive attempt to implement a fully distributed, content-centric ad-hoc network for LLM agents. By bridging these two fields, we believe that the proposed RAPS framework does not merely offer a new method, but rather unveils a vast design space at the intersection of classic networking principles and modern MAS designs. Future work may further exploit this isomorphism by introducing concepts such as congestion control (to manage token limits), packet prioritization (for urgent reasoning paths), and hierarchical sub-netting (for massive-scale agent societies).

We provide the pseudocode for the proposed RAPS framework in Algorithm 1. The workflow delineates the interaction between the distributed publish-subscribe substrate and the two overlay mechanisms (Reactive Subscription and Bayesian Reputation) over discrete time steps.

Appendix D Dataset Statistics

We summarize the dataset statistics in Table 6. For general reasoning task, we use the MMLU dataset (Hendrycks et al., 2020) to evaluate the agents’ breadth of knowledge and problem-solving abilities across diverse subjects, ranging from STEM fields to humanities. The tasks involve multiple-choice questions that require the agents to leverage extensive world knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Following standard practices for agent evaluation (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), we utilize a representative test subset to measure the zero-shot accuracy. For mathematical reasoning task, we employ three widely-used datasets (Cobbe et al., 2021; Patel et al., 2021; Ling et al., 2017) to test the system’s capability in multi-step logical reasoning and calculation. For code generation task, we utilize the HumanEval dataset (Chen et al., 2021), which comprises 164 hand-written Python coding problems. Each problem includes a function signature, docstring, and unit tests. This benchmark evaluates the functional correctness of the generated code. We report the Pass@1 metric, which measures the percentage of problems for which the first generated solution passes all unit tests.

Appendix E Implementation Details

Backbone Models

In the main experiments, we employ GPT-4o-mini as the primary LLM backbone to instantiate the Publisher (f𝙿f^{\mathtt{P}}), Subscriber (f𝚂f^{\mathtt{S}}), and Watchdog (f𝙳f^{\mathtt{D}}) functions. For the embedding-based Broker (f𝙱f^{\mathtt{B}}) function, we utilize the text-embedding-3-small model to compute semantic similarity between publications and subscriptions. Moreover, we implement an LLM-driven broker variant powered by GPT-4o-mini for the ablation analysis. Following the previous works (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b), we set the LLM temperature to 0.70.7 for multi-agent models to encourage their diversity.

Hyperparameter Selection

Unless otherwise specified, we fix the agent population size at N=5N=5 and the maximum communication rounds at k=5k=5 across all benchmarks. These choices are determined to balance inference performance with computational efficiency. For the Bayesian reputation update, we set the decay factor λ=0.9\lambda=0.9 to integrate historical trust with recent evidence. In the Broker module, we first retrieve the top-{1, 2, 3} subscribers based on semantic similarity for intent matching, and then filter them with the similarity threshold τsim=0.5\tau_{\text{sim}}=0.5. To ensure robustness, we set the reputation threshold τrep\tau_{\text{rep}} to 0.70.7, where only peers with a reputation expectation below this threshold are considered reliable for communication.

Metrics

Following the standard evaluation protocols (Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025c), we report Accuracy for the MMLU, GSM8K, SVAMP, and AQuA benchmarks. For the HumanEval benchmark, we report the Pass@1 metric, which estimates the probability that the first generated code snippet passes all unit tests.

Agent Configurations

For fair comparisons with prior works (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), we adopt standard role configurations tailored to the specific domain of each benchmark. The initial agent pools are defined as follows: (1) For the general reasoning task (MMLU), we instantiate a diverse panel of five agents including Knowledge Expert, Mathematician, Programmer, Doctor, and Economist; (2) For HumanEval, we employ a software development squad including Project Manager, Algorithm Designer, Programming Expert, Test Analyst, and Bug Fixer; (3) For the mathematical reasoning datasets, we utilize a specialized solver group including Math Solver, Mathematical Analyst, Programming Expert, Inspector, and Final Answerer.

Adversarial Settings

To evaluate robustness, we follow the adversarial protocol from previous studies (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). We attempt to compromise the integrity of the system by altering the system prompt of a subset of agents. Specifically, the predefined helpful role is replaced with a Liar persona. This setting tests the ability of the Bayesian watchdog to identify and isolate malicious actors based on their output quality rather than their declared identity.

Prompts

Appendix F Case Study

To qualitatively validate the coordination dynamics of RAPS, we analyze an execution trace on a complex GSM8K kinematics problem involving variable speeds and direction changes, as detailed in Table 7. The workflow explicitly demonstrates the efficacy of the Reactive Subscription overlay, where agents spontaneously refine their generic role definitions into context-specific intents to align with the evolving message flow. For instance, the Mathematical Analyst (a1a_{1}) evolves its base prompt into a specialized “distance-rate-time” expert to decompose the journey (Step 1), while the Final Answerer (a5a_{5}) specifically tunes its subscription to “displacement and position analysis” (Step 5). This fine-grained adaptation allows a5a_{5} to correctly interpret the “turning around” constraint—calculating the difference (do​u​t−di​nd_{out}-d_{in}) rather than a simple summation—thereby avoiding the context-agnostic errors common in static rigid workflows.

Simultaneously, the trace highlights the system’s robustness against node failures via the Bayesian Reputation overlay. During the parallel execution at Step 3, an adversarial agent (aa​d​va_{adv}) injects a hallucination by assigning a non-zero speed to “standstill traffic”, while the legitimate solver (a3a_{3}) correctly identifies the velocity as zero. RAPS prevents this error from propagating to the final answer through its decentralized trust mechanism: the upstream watchdog evaluates the semantic consistency of both outputs, penalizes the reputation posterior of the adversary, and exclusively routes the verified results from a3a_{3} to the Inspector (a4a_{4}). This isolation capability confirms that RAPS can autonomously secure coordination consistency in open environments without relying on a vulnerable centralized controller.

Appendix G Limitations and Discussion

While RAPS introduces a promising paradigm shift towards adaptive, scalable, and robust coordination for multi-agent systems, several limitations remain inherent to our current design, pointing towards promising avenues for future research.

Dependence on Foundation Model Capabilities

A primary boundary of our framework lies in its reliance on the intrinsic capabilities of the LLM backbones. RAPS operates as a coordination function that optimizes the information flow, but it does not fundamentally alter the reasoning quality of individual agents. Consequently, the system’s performance is constrained by the generative and instruction-following proficiency of the underlying LLMs. If the backbone models inherently lack the necessary domain knowledge, even an optimal routing protocol cannot fully mitigate the generation of low-quality content. Therefore, RAPS stands as an intelligence multiplier that enhances the collective potential of LLM-based agents, rather than a substitute for foundation models. Future improvements in LLM capabilities would further amplify the efficacy of RAPS.

Towards Learnable Coordination Protocols

The RAPS framework operates in a training-free manner, utilizing inference-time LLM prompting to dynamically refine subscriptions and generate publications. While this design ensures high inference efficiency and zero-shot generalization, it leaves room for further optimization on specific task distributions. A promising future direction is to extend RAPS with multi-agent reinforcement learning techniques for optimizing the communicative behaviors of LLM agents. We envision that the distributed reputation scores maintained by local watchdogs may offer a natural source of intrinsic rewards to guide policy evolution towards more trustworthy and collaborative protocols.

Cold Start in Reputation Initialization

The robustness of the RAPS framework relies on the convergence of Bayesian beliefs regarding peer reliability. Nevertheless, akin to many trust-based systems (Buchegger and Le Boudec, 2002), such a reputation accumulation process inherently faces a cold start problem during the initial phase of interaction. At the onset of coordination, the local watchdogs operate with uninformative priors, indicating that the system requires a warm-up period of message exchange to gather sufficient evidence for statistically stable reputation estimates. During these early interactions, the system may remain transiently vulnerable to adversarial agents before they are successfully isolated. To mitigate this, future variants of RAPS could explore reputation transfer mechanisms, where prior beliefs are persisted across different sessions, or employ static profiling to initialize priors based on the inherent risk associated with specific agent roles or tools.

Broadening the Networking Isomorphism

While RAPS successfully validates the efficacy of the publish-subscribe pattern, it represents only a first step in exploiting the deep isomorphism between multi-agent systems and computer networking. The rich history of classic network protocols (Tanenbaum, 2003) offers a vast, largely unexplored design space for future agent coordination. For instance, mechanisms analogous to congestion control (Low et al., 2002) could be adapted to regulate token consumption and prevent context overflow in resource-constrained environments. Similarly, as agent populations scale to massive magnitudes, concepts such as hierarchical subnetting (Kleinrock and Kamoun, 1977) could also be employed to organize agents into functional clusters. We believe that strategically transferring these mature networking primitives to the agentic domain constitutes a fertile ground for designing the next generation of multi-agent architectures.
